title: CLIFT Turns Gemini Robotics On-Device into a Humanoid Specialist
summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA Research posted CLIFT on arXiv on July 31, 2026, one of the first empirical studies of adapting a closed-weight robot foundation model on a real humanoid through a managed fine-tuning API. Working against Gemini Robotics On-Device (GROD), where users submit data and receive a tuned policy with no access to weights, gradients, likelihoods or losses, they find direct supervised fine-tuning through the API already beats a leading open-weight VLA trained on identical demonstrations — but still falls short of mastery on agile, contact-rich tasks. CLIFT (Closed-Loop Iterative Fine-Tuning) closes that gap by converting deployment-time reward feedback into API-compatible supervised data, using a preference-calibrated dense reward model and retrieval-based advantage conditioning. Two flywheel cycles push GROD to near-perfect success without ever opening the model box.
whyItMatters: Robot foundation models are following language models behind an API wall, which leaves downstream users with imitation only — no reinforcement learning, no closed-loop improvement, exactly the tools that agile contact-rich humanoid work needs most. CLIFT shows the wall is thinner than it looks: reward signal can be smuggled into a pure-SFT interface by reshaping it as supervised data. That makes the managed-API regime a viable path for labs and companies that will never train their own foundation model, and it sets the pattern others will copy as more robot models ship closed.
